heuristics.rule: Compare savings rate and PPP-adjusted net savings, not gross salary
heuristics.condition: When evaluating whether a US salary is financially superior to a home-country offer
heuristics.action: Build a line-by-line deduction model for both scenarios and convert to comparable units using PPP factors before concluding
heuristics.because: Gross salary comparisons systematically overstate the US advantage by ignoring taxes, housing, immigration costs, and purchasing power differences that can flip the outcome

heuristics.rule: 401k contributions are not liquid savings — treat them separately in the comparison
heuristics.condition: When calculating actual annual net savings in the US scenario
heuristics.action: Separate 401k balance from liquid savings; count it as a distinct long-term asset locked until 59½, not as spendable wealth
heuristics.because: Including 401k in net savings overstates short-term financial flexibility and conflates wealth accumulation with accessible capital

heuristics.rule: PPP adjustment applies only to local goods, not to USD-denominated or internationally priced items
heuristics.condition: When using PPP to make home-country savings look comparable to US savings
heuristics.action: Apply PPP only to food, domestic services, and local rent; keep international school fees, imported goods, US assets, and international travel at nominal exchange rates
heuristics.because: Overapplying PPP inflates the apparent value of home-country savings and produces an artificially favorable comparison for returning

heuristics.rule: If the two financial outcomes are within 10–20% of each other, stop optimizing the math and shift to non-financial variables
heuristics.condition: When a stay-vs-return model produces results that are close but not definitively one-sided
heuristics.action: Treat the financial question as resolved and make the decision on family proximity, career ceiling, reverse culture shock risk, and sense of belonging
heuristics.because: Within a 10–20% band, financial projections are within modeling error and life quality variables have larger actual impact on outcomes

heuristics.rule: Include immigration legal fees as a recurring annual cost in the US scenario, not a one-time expense
heuristics.condition: When comparing ongoing cost of living in the US during H-1B or green card processing years
heuristics.action: Add $5,000–$15,000/year for immigration legal costs to the US deduction column as a recurring line item
heuristics.because: These fees are paid annually during the multi-year H-1B and green card process and materially reduce net savings but are routinely omitted from comparisons

decision_factors.why_it_matters: This is the actual unit of wealth accumulation; gross salary comparisons are misleading and this is the corrected metric
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Run the full deduction template for both scenarios, convert home-country savings using PPP factors for local goods only, and compare as a percentage of gross

decision_factors.factor: State income tax in US location
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Ranges from 0% to 13.3%, creating up to a $20K+ annual difference for the same job depending on state — this alone can swing the savings rate comparison
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify the specific state; apply the correct marginal and effective rate to the gross salary in the model

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Rent in major US tech hubs runs $30K–$66K/year and is the single largest post-tax expenditure, often exceeding the tax burden
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Use current market rent for a realistic unit size (not minimum) in the actual city of employment, not national averages

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Childcare in US cities adds $18K–$42K/year per child; international school in China adds ¥200K–¥350K/year — these costs can eliminate savings entirely in either scenario
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine number of children, ages, and schooling needs; apply city-specific childcare or international school cost to the relevant scenario

decision_factors.why_it_matters: RMB and INR have experienced significant depreciation vs. USD in certain periods; savings in local currency may lose real value relative to USD-denominated wealth
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Review 10-year historical exchange rate trajectory for the home currency; assess whether savings will remain in local currency or be converted

decision_factors.why_it_matters: H-1B and green card legal fees of $5K–$15K/year reduce US net savings materially and represent a cost with no equivalent in the home-country scenario
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine current visa stage and expected timeline to green card; annualize total projected legal and filing costs over that period

decision_factors.why_it_matters: The inability to freely switch employers without visa risk limits career optionality and may suppress compensation growth relative to what a free agent could achieve
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess how close you are to green card; determine whether your employer and role constrain your ability to pursue better offers

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Local stock market and real estate returns determine whether home-country savings compound effectively; Chinese real estate has been in a downturn 2023–2025
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research current and historical returns for home-country equity and real estate markets; compare to US equity market baseline

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Tax filing for departure year, cross-border CPA fees, income gap during job search, and relocation costs can total $20K–$50K+ in the return year
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Enumerate: departure-year tax filing cost, months of expected job search gap, relocation costs, and any covered expatriate tax exposure

decision_factors.factor: US network maintenance cost if returning
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Preserving professional relationships in the US after return requires $5K–$15K/year in travel costs that reduce the financial benefit of returning
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Estimate number of trips per year needed to maintain relevant US professional relationships and price at current airfare

hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The money reduces current tax liability but is illiquid until age 59½ — it inflates apparent savings while reducing actual financial flexibility for life decisions before retirement age
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Professionals in their 30s–40s who may need capital for a home purchase, business investment, or international relocation before retirement

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying in a high-cost US city for a high gross salary
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: After federal tax, state tax, FICA, rent, healthcare, and immigration fees, the net liquid savings can be lower than a mid-tier home-country role — but the gross number creates a persistent illusion of wealth accumulation
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Single professionals in California or New York comparing offers without running the full deduction model

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Returning to home country with children of school age
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: International school fees of $15K–$50K/year per child can consume most or all of the savings advantage that the home-country role appeared to offer
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Families with two or more school-age children who assume lower cost of living in the home country will translate to higher savings

hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Currency depreciation can silently erode the real value of those savings relative to USD-denominated wealth over a 10–20 year horizon, even if nominal savings rates look comparable
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Professionals who plan to eventually purchase US assets or retire with USD-denominated costs

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Omitting immigration legal fees from US cost modeling
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The US scenario is systematically overstated in its savings potential; the multi-year legal process costs $5K–$15K/year and reduces the actual net savings rate by 5–15% at mid-level salaries
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: H-1B holders in early green card processing who treat immigration as a sunk cost rather than an ongoing annual expense

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Applying PPP adjustment to all home-country expenses
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Internationally priced goods — electronics, imported items, international schooling, international travel — do not benefit from PPP and will cost the same or more in home-country terms, making the effective purchasing power lower than the adjusted figure suggests
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Professionals who consume a high proportion of internationally priced goods or plan international travel frequently

failure_patterns.pattern: Comparing gross salaries across countries without running a deduction model
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Gross salary is the most visible and easily comparable number; the deduction cascade requires effort and country-specific knowledge that most people lack
failure_patterns.consequence: The person concludes the US option is financially dominant when net savings rates may be comparable or even favor the home country after full accounting
warning_signs: Person states their US salary is '2–3x higher' without mentioning tax rates or housing costs
Person has never calculated their actual annual liquid savings number

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating 401k balance as equivalent to liquid savings
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: 401k appears on net worth statements and reduces tax bills, creating the cognitive impression that it is available wealth
failure_patterns.consequence: Person overestimates their actual financial position and underestimates how little liquid capital they are accumulating annually
warning_signs: Person cites combined 401k + liquid savings as a single net savings figure
Person plans to use retirement funds for near-term goals like home purchase or relocation

failure_patterns.pattern: Applying PPP adjustment uniformly to all home-country costs and savings
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: PPP is taught as a general correction for purchasing power and people apply it broadly without understanding its scope limitations
failure_patterns.consequence: Home-country savings are overstated; actual purchasing power for imported goods, international schooling, and travel is lower than the adjusted figure implies
warning_signs: Person claims their home-country salary 'effectively' equals their US salary after PPP
Person's lifestyle involves significant imported goods, international schools, or frequent international travel

failure_patterns.pattern: Excluding one-time return transition costs from the comparison
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: These costs are in the future, uncertain, and psychologically feel separate from the steady-state financial comparison
failure_patterns.consequence: The financial benefit of returning is overstated in year one and potentially year two; person may face a capital crunch during transition
warning_signs: Person's return plan does not account for income gap during job search
Person has not consulted a cross-border CPA about departure-year tax obligations

failure_patterns.pattern: Continuing to optimize the financial model after both scenarios are within 10–20% of each other
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Financial modeling feels objective and controllable; non-financial variables like belonging and culture feel subjective and hard to weigh
failure_patterns.consequence: Person delays decision or makes it on marginal financial differences that are within modeling error, while ignoring variables that will dominate their actual life satisfaction
warning_signs: Person keeps asking for more precise tax calculations when scenarios are already close
Person avoids discussing family, culture, or career ceiling factors in the decision

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your actual annual liquid savings number — after all taxes, rent, healthcare, and immigration fees?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person has run a real deduction model or is reasoning from gross salary; reveals actual financial accumulation rate
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What percentage of gross is that, and have you included immigration legal fees as a recurring line item?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Walk through the deduction template together before making any financial comparison to a home-country scenario

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have children, and if so, are they school-age?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether international school fees need to be modeled in the home-country scenario, which can eliminate the savings advantage of returning
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: How many children, and have you priced international school fees in the specific city you would return to?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Do you plan to have children within the 5-year horizon of this decision, and if so, in which country?

diagnostic_questions.question: Which US state are you in, or would you be in?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: State income tax rate, which ranges from 0% to 13.3% and can shift the net savings comparison by $15K–$25K annually at high incomes
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Are you in California or New York? If so, the combined federal and state tax burden makes the US savings rate significantly lower than the gross suggests.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If Texas or Florida, the no-state-income-tax advantage materially improves the US scenario and should be explicitly modeled

diagnostic_questions.question: Where will your savings be held and in what currency — and have you modeled currency depreciation risk?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person understands that nominally equal savings in local currency may lose real value against USD over a 10–20 year horizon
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you looked at the 10-year historical trajectory of that currency against USD, and does your plan depend on converting back to USD at any point?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Review historical RMB or INR depreciation periods against USD before treating local savings as equivalent to USD savings

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you consulted a cross-border CPA about departure-year US tax obligations?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person has accounted for the one-time cost of exit — departure-year filing complexity, potential covered expatriate status, and transition-year income gaps
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is the estimated all-in cost of the transition year, and is it included in your return scenario model?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: This is a required step before finalizing any return plan; the cost ranges from $3K to significantly higher and is frequently omitted from comparisons

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the home-country gross salary in USD at current exchange rates, and what is the effective income tax rate at that level?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person knows their actual home-country net income or is reasoning from a nominal figure without applying local tax rates
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you applied the correct progressive tax bracket for that income level in the specific country and city?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: China's IIT at ¥600K is approximately ¥120K–¥150K — the effective rate is significant and must be modeled, not assumed to be low

industry_realities.common_belief: A $200K US salary is obviously superior to any home-country equivalent because it's 2–3× higher in gross terms
industry_realities.actual_reality: After federal tax, California state tax, FICA, San Francisco rent, healthcare, and immigration legal fees, $200K in SF may yield only $62K in liquid annual savings — which can be comparable to or lower than a well-compensated home-country role in PPP-adjusted terms
industry_realities.implication: Never compare gross salaries across countries; always run the full deduction model to net liquid savings before drawing conclusions

industry_realities.common_belief: PPP adjustment makes home-country salaries comparable to US salaries across the board
industry_realities.actual_reality: PPP applies only to locally produced goods and services; internationally priced items — electronics, imported goods, international schools, international travel — are priced at or near global rates and do not benefit from PPP
industry_realities.implication: Segment your spending into local and international buckets before applying PPP; professionals with internationally oriented lifestyles will find their effective PPP benefit is significantly lower than headline figures suggest

industry_realities.common_belief: 401k savings are real savings that count toward your financial position
industry_realities.actual_reality: 401k funds are locked until age 59½ (with 10% penalty plus taxes for early withdrawal); for professionals making major life decisions in their 30s and 40s, this capital is not available and should not be treated as equivalent to liquid savings
industry_realities.implication: Maintain two separate mental accounts: liquid annual savings (decision-relevant) and retirement accumulation (long-term); compare scenarios on the liquid number

industry_realities.common_belief: Immigration fees are a one-time cost that you pay once and forget
industry_realities.actual_reality: H-1B and green card legal and filing fees recur annually over a multi-year process, typically totaling $5K–$15K/year during the green card processing period, which can last 5–15+ years
industry_realities.implication: Model immigration costs as a recurring annual line item in the US scenario for as long as you remain in the green card queue, not as a sunk cost or one-time expense

industry_realities.common_belief: Home-country real estate is a reliable wealth-building vehicle that improves the financial case for returning
industry_realities.actual_reality: Chinese real estate has been in a significant downturn as of 2023–2025; historical strong performance does not guarantee future returns, and local real estate markets carry country-specific regulatory and economic risks
industry_realities.implication: Do not assume home-country real estate will replicate past performance; model real estate appreciation conservatively and separately from the salary comparison

industry_realities.common_belief: The financial comparison between staying and returning will clearly favor one option
industry_realities.actual_reality: After running a complete model, many people find the two scenarios are within 10–20% of each other financially — the model's value is in removing false certainty, not in producing a clear winner
industry_realities.implication: Expect the model to narrow the decision to a range, not resolve it; prepare to make the final call on non-financial variables rather than waiting for the math to decide

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Compares gross salary figures across countries and concludes the higher gross number represents greater wealth accumulation
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Builds a line-by-line deduction model for both scenarios and compares net liquid savings rates in PPP-adjusted terms
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Gross salary comparisons can invert the actual financial outcome; the person who looks financially ahead may be saving less in real terms

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Counts 401k contributions as part of annual savings and feels financially ahead because of growing retirement balance
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Separates 401k into a distinct long-term illiquid asset category and focuses on liquid annual savings for near-term decision-making
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Conflating locked and liquid savings produces false confidence in financial position and distorts the stay-vs-return comparison

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Applies PPP broadly to conclude that home-country salary 'effectively' equals US salary, without distinguishing local vs. internationally priced goods
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Applies PPP selectively to locally produced goods and services; keeps internationally priced items at nominal exchange rates; notes the caveat explicitly in the model
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Overapplying PPP inflates the apparent value of home-country savings and leads to overconfidence in the return scenario

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Models salary, rent, and taxes; omits immigration legal fees, childcare, international school costs, and return transition costs
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Enumerates all material cost categories including immigration fees, children's education, one-time transition costs, and ongoing network maintenance travel
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Omitted costs systematically bias the comparison; the omissions are not random — they tend to understate the true cost of staying in the US and understate the one-time cost of returning

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Decision timing relative to model output
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Keeps refining the financial model looking for a definitive answer, treating non-financial factors as secondary until the math resolves
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Recognizes when two scenarios are within modeling error (10–20%), stops optimizing the financial model, and shifts decision weight to non-financial variables
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Excessive financial modeling in a close-outcome scenario is a form of decision avoidance; the factors that will dominate life satisfaction are being deprioritized

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Converts home-country savings to USD at current exchange rate and treats the result as a stable, comparable figure
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Reviews historical exchange rate volatility, models depreciation scenarios, and treats local-currency savings as carrying currency risk relative to USD-denominated wealth
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A savings rate that looks comparable today may significantly underperform over a 10–20 year horizon if the home currency depreciates, which has happened with both RMB and INR in specific periods
